q: What are the basic standing yoga poses?
How do you do Mountain Pose (Tadasana)?
What is Warrior I (Virabhadrasana I)?
What is Triangle Pose (Trikonasana)?
What is Tree Pose (Vrksasana)?
How do I do Eagle Pose (Garudasana)?
What is Chair Pose (Utkatasana)?
a: Standing poses form the foundation of many yoga practices. Mountain Pose (Tadasana) is the blueprint for all standing poses: feet grounded, legs engaged, core lifted, shoulders relaxed, and arms at sides with palms facing forward—it teaches proper alignment and posture. Warrior I (Virabhadrasana I) involves stepping one foot back with hips squared forward, front knee bent at 90 degrees, and arms reaching overhead. Triangle Pose (Trikonasana) has legs wide apart, front foot forward and back foot at 90 degrees, with one hand reaching down to the shin or floor and the other reaching upward, creating length through the side body. Many standing poses have twisting variations—for example, Revolved Triangle (Parivrtta Trikonasana) adds a spinal twist to the triangle foundation. These poses develop leg strength, hip flexibility, balance, and stability, and are typically sequenced toward the beginning of a practice.

q: What are the main seated forward fold poses?
How do you do Seated Forward Fold (Paschimottanasana)?
What is Bound Angle Pose (Baddha Konasana)?
What is Hero Pose (Virasana)?
What is Lotus Pose (Padmasana)?
How do I sit comfortably for meditation?
a: Seated and forward fold poses develop hip and hamstring flexibility, calm the mind, and prepare the body for meditation. Seated Forward Fold (Paschimottanasana) involves sitting with legs extended, hinging at the hips, and reaching toward the feet while maintaining a long spine. Bound Angle (Baddha Konasana) brings the soles of the feet together, allowing the knees to open outward to stretch the inner thighs and groin. Hero Pose (Virasana) is kneeling with the shins on the floor and sitting between the feet—excellent for digestion and meditation. Lotus (Padmasana) requires significant hip mobility: each foot rests on the opposite thigh, with the spine naturally erect. For those unable to sit on the floor comfortably, Sukhasana (easy cross-legged) on a cushion or sitting in a chair with feet flat are perfectly acceptable alternatives for meditation. Other key seated poses include Staff Pose (Dandasana), Cow Face (Gomukhasana), and Garland (Malasana).

q: What are the main backbend yoga poses?
How do you do Cobra Pose (Bhujangasana)?
What is Upward Facing Dog (Urdhva Mukha Svanasana)?
What is Wheel Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana)?
What is Camel Pose (Ustrasana)?
How do I safely practice backbends?
What is Bow Pose (Dhanurasana)?
a: Backbends open the front body, strengthen the back, improve posture, and can be energizing and emotionally releasing. Cobra Pose (Bhujangasana) is a gentle backbend from prone, lifting the chest with the hands under the shoulders and elbows hugging the ribs—a beginner-friendly spinal extension. Upward Facing Dog (Urdhva Mukha Svanasana) is more intense, using arm strength to lift the thighs off the mat while keeping the shoulders over the wrists. Camel Pose (Ustrasana) is a kneeling backbend reaching back toward the heels, requiring hip and spine flexibility. Wheel Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana) is a full backbend from supine, pressing the entire body upward into a deep arch—strongly engaging the glutes, shoulders, and spine extensors. Safety principles for backbends include warming up the spine thoroughly (cat/cow, gentle circles), engaging the glutes to protect the lower back, drawing the front ribs in to avoid overarching the lumbar spine, and never forcing or jerking into depth. Bridge Pose (Setu Bandha Sarvangasana) is an excellent preparatory and therapeutic backbend.

q: What are the main inversion poses in yoga?
How do I do Headstand (Sirsasana)?
What is Shoulderstand (Sarvangasana)?
What is Handstand (Adho Mukha Vrksasana)?
What are the benefits of inversions?
Who should not do inversions?
a: Inversions are poses where the head is below the heart, offering circulatory, lymphatic, and nervous system benefits. Headstand (Sirsasana) is often called the 'king of asanas'—it can be practiced with the forearms on the floor, hands interlaced, and the crown of the head resting lightly. Tripod headstand has the hands and head forming a triangle base. Shoulderstand (Sarvangasana) uses the shoulders as the base with the legs vertical, often supported by blankets under the shoulders and a wall or chair for support. Handstand (Adho Mukha Vrksasana) requires significant shoulder opening, core strength, and balance—practice against a wall first. Downward Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana) is a gentle inversion accessible to most practitioners. Inversions are contraindicated for those with high blood pressure, glaucoma (increased intraocular pressure is risky), neck injuries, and during pregnancy (especially after the first trimester). Always practice near a wall and learn with a qualified teacher before attempting unsupported inversions.

q: What are the benefits of backbends?
What are backbend poses for flexibility?
What are the safety considerations for backbends?
How do I open my chest with backbends?
What are beginner-friendly backbends?
a: Backbends counteract the forward-curved posture of modern life (sitting at desks, looking at phones), opening the chest, shoulders, and hip flexors while strengthening the spinal extensors. Beginner-friendly backbends include Sphinx Pose (forearms on the floor, gentle lift of the chest), Cobra (Bhujangasana), and a supported backbend over a bolster or rolled blanket placed under the upper back. More advanced backbends include Bow Pose (Dhanurasana—pulling the ankles while prone), King Pigeon (Eka Pada Rajakapotasana—a deep hip opener and backbend combined), and Dropbacks from standing. Chest openers specific to backbend preparation include standing backbend (Anuvittasana), Crescent Lunge with a backbend, and using a yoga wheel or over a chair for supported opening. Safety precautions include avoiding compression in the lower back by engaging the glutes and drawing the front ribs toward the pelvis, maintaining neck length, and warming up for 15-20 minutes before deeper backbends.
